claim: Sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) are one of the most synchronous events of the brain.
source: Local field potential (LFP) deflections and oscillations define hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWRs), one of the most synchronous events of the brain.
evidence: This is a characterization statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about SWRs.

claim: SWRs reflect firing and synaptic current sequences emerging from cognitively relevant neuronal ensembles.
source: SWRs reflect firing and synaptic current sequences emerging from cognitively relevant neuronal ensembles.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific understanding of SWR physiology.

claim: One-dimensional convolutional networks operating over high-density LFP hippocampal recordings allowed for automatic identification of SWR from the rodent hippocampus.
source: Here, we show how one-dimensional convolutional networks operating over high-density LFP hippocampal recordings allowed for automatic identification of SWR from the rodent hippocampus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The CNN discovered physiologically relevant processes associated to the emergence of SWR when applied without retraining to new datasets and ultra-dense hippocampus-wide recordings.
source: When applied without retraining to new datasets and ultra-dense hippocampus-wide recordings, we discovered physiologically relevant processes associated to the emergence of SWR, prompting for novel classification criteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from applying the trained CNN to Neuropixels recordings and external datasets.

claim: The artificial network relied on feature-based specialization to identify spatially segregated oscillations and deflections, as well as synchronous population firing typical of replay.
source: We found it relied in feature-based specialization, which permit identification of spatially segregated oscillations and deflections, as well as synchronous population firing typical of replay.
evidence: This finding is supported by the saliency map analysis and kernel weight visualization presented in the Results section.

claim: Biologically relevant oscillations are considered reliable markers of brain operation.
source: Biologically relevant oscillations are considered reliable markers of brain operation (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Friston et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Analysis of either surface electroencephalography (EEG) or intracranial local field potential (LFP) is typically based on spectral methods relying on gold-standard definitions.
source: Thus, analysis of either surface electroencephalography (EEG) or intracranial local field potential (LFP) is typically based on spectral methods relying on gold-standard definitions (Niedermeyer and Silva, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature on EEG/LFP analysis methods.

claim: Features of EEG/LFP signals such as the slope, polarity, and latency to events are equally important as spectral features.
source: However, other features of EEG/LFP signals such as the slope, polarity, and latency to events are equally important (Modi and Sahin, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: During memory consolidation and retrieval, the hippocampal system releases short memory traces in the form of neuronal sequences.
source: During memory consolidation and retrieval, the hippocampal system releases short memory traces in the form of neuronal sequences (Joo and Frank, 2018; Pfeiffer, 2020; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Neuronal sequences come often in tandem with spatially segregated oscillations (100–250 Hz) and LFP deflections dubbed sharp-wave ripples (SWRs).
source: Such activity comes often in tandem with spatially segregated oscillations (100–250 Hz) and LFP deflections dubbed sharp-wave ripples (SWRs) (Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: SWRs result from active recruitment of dedicated cell-type-specific microcircuits.
source: They result from active recruitment of dedicated cell-type-specific microcircuits (de la Prida, 2020; Stark et al., 2014; Valero et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SWR-associated sequences can either replay previous experience or preplay internal representations.
source: SWR-associated sequences can either replay previous experience or preplay internal representations (Farooq and Dragoi, 2019; Foster, 2017; Joo and Frank, 2018), making their automatic detection crucial in understanding memory function.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Spectral-based filters have permitted real-time SWR-related interventions.
source: However, while spectral-based filters have permitted real-time SWR-related interventions (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Girardeau et al., 2009; Jadhav et al., 2012), these methods are not optimal to disambiguate the underlying variability of a wealth of events, especially during online operation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating real-time interventions.

claim: Spectral-based filter methods are not optimal to disambiguate the underlying variability of SWR events, especially during online operation.
source: However, while spectral-based filters have permitted real-time SWR-related interventions (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Girardeau et al., 2009; Jadhav et al., 2012), these methods are not optimal to disambiguate the underlying variability of a wealth of events, especially during online operation.
evidence: This is a critical assessment based on the authors' understanding of the field and is supported by inference from the literature.

claim: With the advent of ultra-dense recordings, the need for automatic identification of SWR is pressing.
source: Moreover, with the advent of ultra-dense recordings, the need for automatic identification is pressing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of technology and the challenges it presents.

claim: Current solutions for SWR detection still require improvement to capture the complexity of SWR events across hippocampal layers.
source: In spite of recent advances (Dutta et al., 2019; Hagen et al., 2021), current solutions still require improvement to capture the complexity of SWR events across hippocampal layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work and inference about their limitations.

claim: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have extraordinary capability for real-time recognition.
source: Here, we exploit the extraordinary capability of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for real-time recognition to identify SWR (Bai et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work on CNNs.

claim: The one-dimensional CNN operating over high-density LFP hippocampal signals overcomes spectral methods in detecting a large variety of SWR.
source: We show how one-dimensional CNN operating over high-density LFP hippocampal signals overcome spectral methods in detecting a large variety of SWR.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing CNN and filter performance.

claim: The CNN was trained using a dataset manually tagged by an expert for training and initial validation (1794 events, two sessions from two mice).
source: Having defined the main network architecture, we used a dataset manually tagged by an expert for training and initial validation (1794 events, two sessions from two mice; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the training data used in the study.

claim: The start and the end of SWR events were manually annotated so that the CNN could learn their onset.
source: An important decision we made was manually annotating the start and the end of SWR events so that the CNN could learn their onset.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision in the study.

claim: The offline performance of CNN12 and CNN32 was better than the Butterworth filter as compared using the P-R curve.
source: The P-R curve depicted better offline operation of both the CNN12 and CNN32 as compared with the filter (Figure 2A, left).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The CNN was more robust than the filter when considering the relationship between performance and the detection threshold.
source: When we considered the relationship between performance and the detection threshold, we found that the CNN was more robust than the filter (Figure 2A, right).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Filter thresholds had effect in biasing detection of SWR, which exhibited different mean feature values (frequency and power).
source: Filter thresholds had effect in biasing detection of SWR, which exhibited different mean feature values (frequency and power) (Figure 2B, upper plots).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mean features of SWR detected by the CNN did not depend on the threshold and were consistent with the ground truth.
source: In contrasts, mean features of SWR detected by the CNN did not depend on the threshold and were consistent with the ground truth (Figure 2B, bottom).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The CNN at 12.8 ms resolution exhibited better online performance compared with the filter (per session p=0.0047; per mice p=0.033).
source: We found better online performance of the CNN at 12.8 ms resolution as compared with the filter (Figure 2C; per session p=0.0047; per mice p=0.033).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of online detection data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The CNN slightly overtook the Butterworth filter in the ability to anticipate SWR events online (time-to-SWR-peak for CNN12: –7.01±2.05 ms; Butterworth filter: –4.66±2.87 ms; paired t-test, p=0.048).
source: When it came to the ability to anticipate SWR events online, the CNN slightly overtook the Butterworth filter (time-to-SWR-peak for CNN12: –7.01±2.05 ms; Butterworth filter: –4.66±2.87 ms; paired t-test, p=0.048).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of timing data.

claim: When using the best possible detection threshold per session, CNN and filter exhibited roughly similar F1 values (CNN12: F1=0.68 ± 0.06; CNN32: F1=0.63 ± 0.05; Butterworth filter: F1=0.65 ± 0.11).
source: To this purpose, we equated the methods using the best possible detection threshold per session (the one that optimized F1) and found roughly similar values (Figure 3A; CNN12: F1=0.68 ± 0.06; CNN32: F1=0.63 ± 0.05; Butterworth filter: F1=0.65 ± 0.11), indicating the CNN meet the gold standard provided the filter is optimized.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The filter exhibited larger variability across sessions compared to the CNN.
source: Remarkably, the filter exhibited larger variability across sessions.
evidence: This observation is inferred from the data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The CNN performed similar to a filter-based optimized algorithm (F1=0.65 ± 0.11).
source: Our CNN performed similar to a filter-based optimized algorithm (F1=0.65 ± 0.11) (Dutta et al., 2019), but significantly better than RippleNET, a recurrent network designed to detect SWR mostly during periods of immobility (F1=0.31 ± 0.22; p<0.00001 one-way ANOVA for comparisons with both CNN12 and CNN32) (Hagen et al., 2021).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data from the study and citations to prior work.

claim: The CNN performed significantly better than RippleNET (F1=0.31 ± 0.22; p<0.00001 one-way ANOVA for comparisons with both CNN12 and CNN32).
source: Our CNN performed similar to a filter-based optimized algorithm (F1=0.65 ± 0.11) (Dutta et al., 2019), but significantly better than RippleNET, a recurrent network designed to detect SWR mostly during periods of immobility (F1=0.31 ± 0.22; p<0.00001 one-way ANOVA for comparisons with both CNN12 and CNN32) (Hagen et al., 2021).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis comparing CNN and RippleNET performance, with citation to the RippleNET paper.

claim: When confronted with the consolidated ground truth from two experts, the CNN could be actually detecting many more SWR events than initially accounted by each individual expert (one-way ANOVA for ground truth, CNN12: F(2)=0.01, p=0.026; CNN32: F(2)=0.01, p=0.013).
source: Interestingly, when we confronted the network detection with the consolidated ground truth, we noted that the CNN could be actually detecting many more SWR events than initially accounted by each individual expert (one-way ANOVA for ground truth, CNN12: F(2)=0.01, p=0.026; CNN32: F(2)=0.01, p=0.013).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of detection performance against different ground truths.

claim: The filter failed to exhibit improvement when tested against the consolidated ground truth, and performed worse (one-way ANOVA for models, F(2)=0.02, p=0.033).
source: In contrast, the filter failed to exhibit such an improvement, and performed worse when tested against the consolidated ground truth (one-way ANOVA for models, F(2)=0.02, p=0.033) (Figure 3B, rightmost).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An expert acting as a classifier of the other expert's ground truth scored at 0.70±0.13.
source: Notably, an expert acting as a classifier of the other expert's ground truth scored at 0.70±0.13 (Figure 3C), providing mean reference of best performance (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A CNN trained in data from head-fixed mice was able to generalize to freely moving rats.
source: Importantly, a CNN trained in data from head-fixed mice was able to generalize to freely moving rats.
evidence: This finding is supported by the analysis of the external dataset from freely moving rats.

claim: The network recalled most of the annotated events in the external dataset (R=0.80 ± 0.18), but precision was apparently low (P=0.42 ± 0.18).
source: Consistently, the network recalled most of the annotated events (R=0.80 ± 0.18), but precision was apparently low (P=0.42 ± 0.18) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Many False Positive predictions in the external dataset were actually unannotated SWR (2403 events), meaning that precision was actually higher (P=0.77 ± 0.08 for CNN32, P=0.86 ± 0.08 for CNN12, both at P<0.01 for paired t-test).
source: Hence, we evaluated all False Positive predictions and found that many of them were actually unannotated SWR (2403 events), meaning that precision was actually higher (P=0.77 ± 0.08 for CNN32, P=0.86 ± 0.08; for CNN12, both at P<0.01 for paired t-test; Figure 3E).
evidence: This finding is supported by manual validation of False Positives and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Detection limits of SWR may be determined by the expert's criteria.
source: Altogether, our analyses indicate that detection limits of SWR may be determined by the expert's criteria.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the analyses comparing different expert annotations and CNN performance.

claim: CNN performance improves when confronted with the consolidated ground truth.
source: CNN performance improves when confronted with the consolidated ground truth, supporting that shared community tagging may help to advance our understanding of SWR definition.
evidence: This finding is supported by the data comparing CNN performance against individual and consolidated ground truths.

claim: Kernels from the first layers specialized in detecting rhythmic and periodic patterns.
source: Consistently with data above, kernels from the first layers specialized in detecting rhythmic and periodic patterns (e.g. L1K1 and L1K2), while later layers seem to focus in identifying these patterns along time (e.g. L19K18; Figure 4B).
evidence: This finding is supported by the saliency map analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Later layers of the CNN seem to focus in identifying patterns along time.
source: Consistently with data above, kernels from the first layers specialized in detecting rhythmic and periodic patterns (e.g. L1K1 and L1K2), while later layers seem to focus in identifying these patterns along time (e.g. L19K18; Figure 4B).
evidence: This finding is supported by the saliency map analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: L1K1 was maximally activated at the peak of ripple oscillations.
source: For example, L1K1 was maximally activated at the peak of ripple oscillations, while L1K2 and L19K18 were maximal at the onset, supporting the network ability to anticipate SWR.
evidence: This finding is supported by the pattern-matching analysis between saliency maps and LFP inputs.

claim: L1K2 and L19K18 were maximal at the onset of SWR, supporting the network ability to anticipate SWR.
source: For example, L1K1 was maximally activated at the peak of ripple oscillations, while L1K2 and L19K18 were maximal at the onset, supporting the network ability to anticipate SWR.
evidence: This finding is supported by the pattern-matching analysis and provides inference about the network's predictive capability.

claim: Pattern-matching was maximal for True Positive and minimal for True Negative events (one-way ANOVA, F(3)=1517, p<0.0001).
source: Consistent with the examples, pattern-matching was maximal for True Positive and minimal for True Negative events (one-way ANOVA, F(3)=1517, p<0.0001).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of pattern-matching values.

claim: Pattern-matching values were higher for False Positives than for False Negatives.
source: Pattern-matching values were higher for False Positives than for False Negatives (Figure 4E), meaning that the network may be identifying some latent features.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and suggests inference about latent features.

claim: About 20% of False Positive predictions could be reclassified into physiologically relevant categories.
source: A closer examination of False Positive predictions suggested that about 20% of them could be reclassified.
evidence: This finding is supported by manual examination of False Positive events.

claim: About one-third of reclassifiable False Positives were sharp waves without clear associated ripples (SW no ripples).
source: From these, about one-third were sharp waves without clear associated ripples (SW no ripples), while others were actually ripples events without associated sharp waves (ripples no SW), population firing, and artifacts (Figure 4F).
evidence: This finding is supported by manual categorization of False Positives shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Examination of False Positive by the filter showed a major trend to detect artifacts at the expenses of more physiologically relevant events.
source: Instead, examination of False Positive by the filter showed a major trend to detect artifacts at the expenses of more physiologically relevant events (Figure 4F).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The CNN has the ability to identify SWR events by relying on feature-based kernel operation.
source: This analysis confirms that the CNN has the ability to identify SWR events by relying on feature-based kernel operation.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the saliency map and pattern-matching analyses.

claim: Some ambiguous predictions according to the current definition of SWR may identify different forms of population firing and oscillatory activities associated to sharp waves.
source: Moreover, some ambiguous predictions according to the current definition of SWR may identify different forms of population firing and oscillatory activities associated to sharp waves, supporting the network ability to generalize beyond the particular expert's ground truth.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the analysis of False Positive events and their physiological characteristics.

claim: L1K1 acted along the spatial scale by differentially weighting LFP channels along the somatodendritic axis and deep-superficial layers.
source: For example, L1K1 acted along the spatial scale by differentially weighting LFP channels along the somatodendritic axis and deep-superficial layers (Figure 6A), consistent with the saliency map shown above.
evidence: This finding is supported by visualization of kernel weights shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Weights from L1K2 likely operated in the temporal scale with major differences along the kernel length.
source: In contrast, weights from L1K2 likely operated in the temporal scale with major differences along the kernel length (Figure 6A).
evidence: This finding is supported by visualization of kernel weights shown in Figure 6A.

claim: UMAP successfully segregated feature maps of LFP events according to their detection probability in a two-dimensional cloud.
source: UMAP successfully segregated feature maps of LFP events according to their detection probability in a two-dimensional cloud (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), supporting that the entire CNN is coding for different features of SWR across layers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This finding is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 6C and supplement.

claim: True Positive and True Negative events fell apart in the UMAP cloud, showing striking segregation.
source: We found striking segregation across the UMAP cloud with True Positive and True Negative events falling apart (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This finding is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 6D.

claim: False Negatives were mostly located at the intermediate region of the UMAP cloud, suggesting they could be detected with less conservative thresholds.
source: False Negatives were mostly located at the intermediate region, suggesting they could be detected with less conservative thresholds.
evidence: This finding is supported by the UMAP visualization and provides inference about threshold effects.

claim: False Positive predictions were scattered all around the UMAP cloud, supporting the idea that they reflect heterogeneous events.
source: Interestingly, False Positive predictions were scattered all around the cloud, supporting the idea that they reflect heterogeneous events as seen above.
evidence: This finding is supported by the UMAP visualization and provides inference about the nature of False Positives.

claim: Validated False Positive events corresponding to population firing synchrony and sharp waves without ripples distributed over the ground truth region in the UMAP cloud, while those corresponding to artifacts mostly fell apart.
source: Mapping all the previously validated False Positive events (see Figure 4F) over the UMAP cloud confirmed that those corresponding to population firing synchrony and sharp waves without ripples distributed over the ground truth, while those corresponding to artifacts mostly fell apart (Figure 6E).
evidence: This finding is supported by the UMAP visualization shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A CNN relying on feature-based detection allows to capture a large diversity of SWR events.
source: Our study suggests that a CNN relying on feature-based detection allows to capture a large diversity of SWR events.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the various analyses of CNN operation and performance.

claim: Detection was optimal at the CA1 cell layer (stratum pyramidale [SP]).
source: While detection was optimal at the CA1 cell layer (stratum pyramidale [SP]), we noted many events were actually identified from SWR-associated LFP signatures at the radiatum (SR) and lacunosum moleculare (SLM) layers (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Many SWR events were identified from SWR-associated LFP signatures at the radiatum (SR) and lacunosum moleculare (SLM) layers.
source: While detection was optimal at the CA1 cell layer (stratum pyramidale [SP]), we noted many events were actually identified from SWR-associated LFP signatures at the radiatum (SR) and lacunosum moleculare (SLM) layers (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 7C and supplement.

claim: Detection of SWR was better at the dorsal than at the ventral hippocampus, except for SR and SLM.
source: When evaluated per layer, detection of SWR was better at the dorsal than at the ventral hippocampus, except for SR and SLM (Figure 7D, left).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Only a subset of SWR could be identified from recordings at SR and SLM (i.e. R-values were low), but precision was very high (i.e. over 80% of predictions were consistent with the ground truth).
source: In spite that only a subset of SWR could be identified from recordings at SR and SLM (i.e. R-values were low), precision was very high (i.e. over 80% of predictions were consistent with the ground truth).
evidence: This finding is supported by the performance metrics from Neuropixels recordings.

claim: Both the Butterworth filter and RippleNET failed to identify SWR-associated signatures beyond the dorsal SP.
source: Remarkably, both the Butterworth filter and RippleNET failed to identify SWR-associated signatures beyond the dorsal SP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 7 supplement.

claim: Larger sinks and sources were found for SWR that can be detected at SLM and SR versus those detected at SO.
source: We found larger sinks and sources for SWR that can be detected at SLM and SR versus those detected at SO (Figure 7G; z-scored by mean values of SWR detected at SP only).
evidence: This finding is supported by CSD analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Pyramidal cells exhibited striking reorganization of the firing rate and timing during SWR detected at SO, SR, and SLM.
source: For pyramidal cells, we found striking reorganization of the firing rate and timing during SWR detected at SO, SR, and SLM (Figure 7H).
evidence: This finding is supported by single-unit analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Timing and rate differences of pyramidal cell and interneuronal firing with respect to SWR events detected at different layers support the idea that they reflect activation of different hippocampal ensembles.
source: Timing and rate differences of pyramidal cell and interneuronal firing with respect to SWR events detected at different layers support the idea that they reflect activation of different hippocampal ensembles.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the firing rate and timing analyses.

claim: One-dimensional convolutional networks operating over high-density LFP recordings allows for improved detection and interpretation of hippocampal SWR events.
source: Here, we report how one-dimensional convolutional networks operating over high-density LFP recordings allows for improved detection and interpretation of hippocampal SWR events.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data presented.

claim: The network was trained in a subset of LFP data recorded around the dorsal CA1 cell layer of head-fixed mice.
source: While the network was trained in a subset of LFP data recorded around the dorsal CA1 cell layer of head-fixed mice, detection generalized across strata, brain locations (e.g. ventral hippocampus), preparations (i.e. freely moving), and species (i.e. rats) without the need for retraining.
evidence: This describes the training data and generalization capability demonstrated in the study.

claim: Detection generalized across strata, brain locations (e.g. ventral hippocampus), preparations (i.e. freely moving), and species (i.e. rats) without the need for retraining.
source: While the network was trained in a subset of LFP data recorded around the dorsal CA1 cell layer of head-fixed mice, detection generalized across strata, brain locations (e.g. ventral hippocampus), preparations (i.e. freely moving), and species (i.e. rats) without the need for retraining.
evidence: This finding is supported by the analyses of Neuropixels recordings and external datasets.

claim: The CNN exhibited a much higher stability, less threshold-dependent sensitivity, and overall higher performance as compared with the spectral filter and RippleNET.
source: Our CNN exhibited a much higher stability, less threshold-dependent sensitivity, and overall higher performance as compared with the spectral filter and RippleNET, a recurrent neural network solution.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the comparative performance analyses throughout the study.

claim: The unique capability of the CNN relies on feature-based analysis of LFP signals, which provide similar explanatory power as standard LFP profiling.
source: This unique capability of our CNN relies on feature-based analysis of LFP signals, which provide similar explanatory power as standard LFP profiling.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the interpretability analyses of CNN operation.

claim: Contributors to gamma oscillations (40–100 Hz) include fluctuating synaptic potentials reflecting inhibition, excitation, or both in interaction with phase-locking firing from subsets of cells.
source: For instance, contributors to gamma oscillations (40–100 Hz) include fluctuating synaptic potentials reflecting inhibition, excitation, or both in interaction with phase-locking firing from subsets of cells (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Bartos et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The specific contribution of the different factors at the resulting dominant oscillatory frequency band is not trivial.
source: The specific contribution of the different factors at the resulting dominant oscillatory frequency band is not trivial (Buzsáki and Schomburg, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Relying on spectral definitions to analyze EEG/LFP data has to cope with the nonstationary nature of brain activity.
source: In addition, relying on spectral definitions to analyze EEG/LFP data has to cope with the nonstationary nature of brain activity, while the demarcation of frequency bands does not necessarily fit to unambiguous basic mechanisms.
evidence: This is a critical assessment based on established knowledge about brain signal analysis.

claim: The demarcation of frequency bands does not necessarily fit to unambiguous basic mechanisms.
source: In addition, relying on spectral definitions to analyze EEG/LFP data has to cope with the nonstationary nature of brain activity, while the demarcation of frequency bands does not necessarily fit to unambiguous basic mechanisms.
evidence: This is a critical assessment based on established knowledge about brain signal analysis.

claim: Recent data suggest pivotal role of entorhinal inputs in modulating and elongating the dynamics of locally generated SWRs.
source: For instance, recent data suggest pivotal role of entorhinal inputs in modulating and elongating the dynamics of locally generated SWRs (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2019; Oliva et al., 2018; Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: SWR events disproportionally weighted by downstream inputs along the CA3 to CA2 axis differentially modulate consolidation of recognition memory at the social and nonsocial domains.
source: Similarly, SWR events disproportionally weighted by downstream inputs along the CA3 to CA2 axis differentially modulate consolidation of recognition memory at the social and nonsocial domains (Nakashiba et al., 2009; Oliva et al., 2020; Oliva et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some ripples can be actually detected at SO, SR, and SLM strata independently on their alleged local generation at the CA1 cell layer.
source: Consistently, we found that some ripples can be actually detected at SO, SR, and SLM strata independently on their alleged local generation at the CA1 cell layer.
evidence: This finding is supported by the Neuropixels recording data.

claim: The configuration of the current sinks and sources associated to independently detected SWR events suggest that the weighted interaction between fluctuating input pathways may entail contribution by different factors across behavioral states.
source: The configuration of the current sinks and sources associated to independently detected SWR events suggest that the weighted interaction between fluctuating input pathways may entail contribution by different factors across behavioral states (Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the CSD data and cited literature.

claim: Different subcircuits may contribute to sleep and awake SWR with different cognitive roles.
source: For instance, different subcircuits may contribute to sleep and awake SWR with different cognitive roles (Roumis and Frank, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The ability to detect ripple oscillations at different layers also indicate a role for dendritic potentials, such as complex spikes and dendritic bursts.
source: The ability to detect ripple oscillations at different layers also indicate a role for dendritic potentials, such as complex spikes and dendritic bursts (Bittner et al., 2015; Kamondi et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection results and supported by citations.

claim: Other GABAergic cells and terminals located at the border between SR and SLM may equally contribute to SWR.
source: Finally, while attention is traditionally focused on parvalbumin and cholecystokinin GABAergic basket cells providing perisomatic innervation (Klausberger et al., 2005), other GABAergic cells and terminals located at the border between SR and SLM may equally contribute (Basu et al., 2016; Kitamura et al., 2015; Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Larger current sources associated with SWR events detected at SLM layers support the contribution of GABAergic cells at the SR-SLM border.
source: This is supported by larger current sources associated with SWR events detected at SLM layers, as we show here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CSD data presented in the study.

claim: Only one part of the dorsal SWR dynamics can be explained locally, consistent with complex interaction along the septotemporal axis.
source: Our data suggest that only one part of the dorsal SWR dynamics can be explained locally, consistent with complex interaction along the septotemporal axis (Patel et al., 2013).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the detection patterns and supported by a citation.

claim: The CNN identify different types of SWR events detected at distant strata suggesting major role of input pathways.
source: Instead, the CNN identify different types of SWR events detected at distant strata suggesting major role of input pathways.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the detection results across hippocampal layers.

claim: A segregated role for dorsal and ventral SWR events suggest that brain-wide subcircuits inherit the different representational dynamics of a variety of replays.
source: A segregated role for dorsal and ventral SWR events suggest that brain-wide subcircuits inherit the different representational dynamics of a variety of replays (Sosa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the detection results and supported by a citation.

claim: The detection unfolding of CNN permit an unbiased categorization without relying on more elusive spectral criteria.
source: The detection unfolding of CNN thus permit an unbiased categorization without relying on more elusive spectral criteria.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the comparative analyses of CNN and spectral methods.

claim: The method identified events beyond the individual expert ground truth.
source: Our method also identified events beyond the individual expert ground truth.
evidence: This finding is supported by the analysis of False Positives and consolidated ground truth.

claim: False Positives reveal sharp waves associated to population firing without ripples, as well as other unclassified forms of activities.
source: Careful examination of those False Positives reveal sharp waves associated to population firing without ripples, as well as other unclassified forms of activities.
evidence: This finding is supported by manual examination of False Positive events.

claim: The ability of CA3 inputs to bring about gamma oscillations and multi-unit firing associated with sharp waves is already recognized.
source: In addition, the ability of CA3 inputs to bring about gamma oscillations and multi-unit firing associated with sharp waves is already recognized (Sullivan et al., 2011), and variability of the ripple power can be related with different cortical subnetworks (Karimi Abadchi et al., 2020; Ramirez-Villegas et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Variability of the ripple power can be related with different cortical subnetworks.
source: In addition, the ability of CA3 inputs to bring about gamma oscillations and multi-unit firing associated with sharp waves is already recognized (Sullivan et al., 2011), and variability of the ripple power can be related with different cortical subnetworks (Karimi Abadchi et al., 2020; Ramirez-Villegas et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Since the power spectral level operationally defines the detection of SWR, part of this microcircuit intrinsic variability may be escaping analysis when using spectral filters.
source: Since the power spectral level operationally defines the detection of SWR, part of this microcircuit intrinsic variability may be escaping analysis when using spectral filters.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the limitations of spectral methods.

claim: Recent data suggest that replay emerging from SWR is more complex than originally thought.
source: Recent data suggest that replay emerging from SWR is more complex than originally thought (Joo and Frank, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Cell-type-specific subcircuits, operating over a variety of interneuronal classes and under the influence of different input pathways, provide mechanistic support for a wealth of SWR events.
source: Cell-type-specific subcircuits, operating over a variety of interneuronal classes and under the influence of different input pathways, provide mechanistic support for a wealth of SWR events (de la Prida, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: SWR detected by gold-standard spectral methods fail to reflect the necessary statistical variance that allows for identifying specific trends.
source: Yet, SWR detected by gold-standard spectral methods fail to reflect the necessary statistical variance that allows for identifying specific trends.
evidence: This is a critical assessment based on the findings of the study.

claim: Relying on unbiased feature-based methods can change the approach to studying SWR.
source: Relying on unbiased feature-based methods hopefully can change the game.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the method.

claim: LFP signals acquired with high-density 8-channel silicon probes provide detailed information about the underlying CA1 microcircuit.
source: LFP signals acquired with high-density 8-channel silicon probes provide detailed information about the underlying CA1 microcircuit (Figure 1A; Mizuseki et al., 2011; Navas-Olive et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The goal of the artificial network operating over 8-channel input signals (down-sampled at 1250 Hz) was to provide a single-output probability for the occurrence of an SWR event in a given temporal window.
source: The goal of the artificial network operating over 8-channel input signals (down-sampled at 1250 Hz) was to provide a single-output probability for the occurrence of an SWR event in a given temporal window (Figure 1A, bottom trace).
evidence: This describes the design goal of the CNN architecture.

claim: The input 'object' is equivalent to a stream of pixels (×1 number of data samples) with 8-channels instead of colors.
source: Therefore, the input 'object' is equivalent to a stream of pixels (×1 number of data samples) with 8-channels instead of colors.
evidence: This describes the conceptual framework for the CNN input.

claim: The CNN architecture was inspired by You-Only-Look-Once (YOLO) networks for real-time object recognition.
source: Inspired by You-Only-Look-Once (YOLO) networks for real-time object recognition (Redmon et al., 2015), we adapted a CNN architecture to search for SWR in the dorsal hippocampus of awake head-fixed mice.
evidence: This describes the inspiration for the CNN architecture with a citation.

claim: The network architecture consists of seven blocks of one Convolutional layer+one BatchNorm layer+one Leaky ReLU layer each (layers 1–21).
source: Network architecture consists of seven blocks of one Convolutional layer+one BatchNorm layer+one Leaky ReLU layer each (layers 1–21).
evidence: This describes the CNN architecture as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dense layer 22 provides the CNN output as the SWR probability.
source: Dense layer 22 provides the CNN output as the SWR probability.
evidence: This describes the final layer of the CNN architecture.

claim: The 8-channel local field potential (LFP) input is progressively transformed to capture different features of the event.
source: Note how the 8-channel local field potential (LFP) input is progressively transformed to capture different features of the event.
evidence: This describes the operation of the CNN as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Some SWR events can be predicted well in advance by the CNN.
source: Note that some events can be predicted well in advance.
evidence: This observation is based on the CNN output shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The 10-best networks exhibited performance F1>0.65 at 32 ms resolution.
source: The resulting 10-best networks exhibited performance F1>0.65 (green scale) at 32 ms resolution.
evidence: This finding is from the preliminary parameter search shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CNN32 exhibited the lowest and more stable learning curve.
source: CNN32 exhibited the lowest and more stable learning curve (arrowhead).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The chosen Butterworth filter parameters were 100–300 Hz bandwidth and order 2.
source: The chosen parameters (100–300 Hz bandwidth and order 2) are indicated by arrowheads.
evidence: This describes the optimized filter parameters shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There was no effect on the number of channels used for the filter (1, 4, and 8 channels).
source: We found no effect on the number of channels used for the filter (1, 4, and 8 channels), and chose that with the higher ripple power.
evidence: This finding is from the filter optimization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The CNN operated in real time at the interface between the Intan recording system and the controller of an opto-electrode probe.
source: CNN operated in real time at the interface between the Intan recording system and the controller of an opto-electrode probe.
evidence: This describes the online detection setup shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Detection was implemented using a plugin designed to incorporate TensorFlow into the OE Graphic User Interface.
source: Detection was implemented using a plugin designed to incorporate TensorFlow into the OE (Siegle et al., 2017) Graphic User Interface https://github.com/PridaLab/CNNRippleDetectorOEPlugin.
evidence: This describes the implementation method with a citation and GitHub link.

claim: All protocols and procedures were performed according to the Spanish legislation (RD 1201/2005 and L.32/2007) and the European Communities Council Directive 2003 (2003/65/CE).
source: All protocols and procedures were performed according to the Spanish legislation (RD 1201/2005 and L.32/2007) and the European Communities Council Directive 2003 (2003/65/CE).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Instituto Cajal and the Spanish Research Council.
source: Experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Instituto Cajal and the Spanish Research Council.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.
